title: The Real Problem Underlying India-China Tensions | NOEMA
gist: A veteran India-China correspondent argues the binding constraint on the post-Galwan India-China reset is not the border or the 5x GDP gap but asymmetric historical memory: China reads India through the colonial 'Ah San' lens of Western subordination, India reads China through the 1962 betrayal. She flags the near-total absence of resident correspondents (one Indian journalist in China, zero Chinese in India as of 2024) as the mechanism that keeps both misreadings intact.

insights.claim: India and China weight each other asymmetrically: Beijing treats India as a regional actor and potential irritant rather than a strategic equal, while China is present in every Indian military procurement decision, border infrastructure project and calculation about Pakistan.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: Asymmetric salience means Indian policy reprices off Chinese moves far more than the reverse — India-exposed defense and border-infrastructure spend is the more reactive leg of the pair.
insights.quote: To China, the U.S. is the only player on the world stage with any real trump cards; the rest of the world, India included, is a supporting cast.
insights.locator: India and China do not think about each other

insights.claim: India and China had similar per capita incomes as recently as 1990, but by 2025 China's GDP of $19.4 trillion was nearly five times India's $4.1 trillion.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: The 5x gap is the hard baseline for any 'India as the next China' allocation thesis and explains why Beijing negotiates from assumed superiority.
insights.locator: As recently as 1990, India and China had similar per capita incomes

insights.claim: At a Beijing dialogue organized by the Center for China and Globalization, a Chinese participant advised Indian journalists that India should accept its relative weakness and learn to leverage China's economic strengths for its own development — advice the Indian side received as condescension rather than pragmatism.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: Register, not substance, is what breaks these talks — a reason to discount headline 'normalization' meetings that lack follow-through mechanisms.
insights.quote: India should accept its position of relative weakness without shame
insights.locator: At the meeting I attended in Beijing

insights.claim: Chinese social media treats India's Vision 2047 developed-nation goal derisively by pointing to Modi's unmet 2019 pledge to build a $5 trillion economy within five years, applying a credibility discount to Indian official targets.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: Indian headline growth targets carry a track-record problem that external counterparties already price in; treat official Indian roadmaps as aspiration, not guidance.
insights.locator: Social media has played an unhelpful role

insights.claim: Chinese perceptions of India have shifted generationally from organic warmth — Hindi films, Buddhism's Indian origin, respect for India's lead in software outsourcing — to viewing India as a laggard to be advised or a presumptuous rival to be put in its place.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: The goodwill floor under the relationship is eroding with generational turnover, so each future crisis starts from a worse baseline than the last.
insights.quote: the view of India seems to have shifted from a potential peer to, at best, a laggard to be advised, or, at worst, a presumptuous rival to be put in its place

insights.claim: Sikh policemen recruited directly from Punjab made up about 12% of the Shanghai Municipal Police from 1885 until the early 1940s, hired because they were cheaper than Europeans and considered more reliable than locals, occupying the role of the colonial enforcer's enforcer.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: The concrete historical basis for Chinese framing of India as a Western instrument — this is the raw material of a durable narrative, not a passing slur.
insights.locator: In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Sikhs

insights.claim: The Shanghainese term hong tou Ah San — 'red-headed number three,' with the British as No. 1 and the Chinese as No. 2 — embedded itself in Chinese usage as a pejorative for Indians generally, carrying a charge of doing the white man’s bidding against fellow Asians.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: Explains why Chinese elites structurally discount Indian claims to independent agency — a bias that will persist through any tactical thaw.
insights.locator: The Shanghainese called the Sikhs hong tou Ah San

insights.claim: Parsi and Marwari merchants were significant commercial intermediaries in the British opium trade into Qing China, with 41 Parsis versus 32 English merchants in Canton's foreign enclave by 1831, widening to 52 Parsis against 35 English traders by 1835.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: Second historical anchor for Chinese resentment of Indian commercial actors; useful context for why Chinese negotiators frame Indian business as an extension of Western interests.
insights.locator: Indian traders, too, had their role

insights.claim: Commercial capital accumulated from the opium trade that devastated China went on to fund the Indian independence movement — the Marwari firm Tarachand Ghanshyamdas traded opium futures across the Malwa belt, and Shivnarain Birla's fortune (grandfather of Gandhi associate G.D. Birla) originated in opium speculation.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: A fact absent from Indian public memory but live in the Chinese frame — the kind of asymmetric history that makes goodwill gestures misfire.
insights.locator: Marwaris supplied a different part of the chain

insights.claim: A significant strand of Chinese opinion reads India's US partnership, Quad membership and closer EU trade ties as a continuation of the colonial subordinate role — and read the 2008 Nuclear Suppliers Group waiver secured by George W. Bush as confirmation that India had settled into being a favored American client rather than as recognition of Indian strategic weight.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: Every Indian move toward Washington or Brussels raises rather than lowers Chinese threat perception, so US-India deepening should be modeled as escalatory for India-China risk, not stabilizing.
insights.quote: Ah San, still doing the white man’s bidding.
insights.locator: When President George W. Bush secured India a waiver

insights.claim: India's founding faith in Asian solidarity — the Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai slogan and the 1954 Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence Nehru invested political capital in — collapsed when China attacked simultaneously in Aksai Chin and the North-East Frontier Agency in October 1962 and India's outnumbered forces collapsed before a unilateral Chinese ceasefire in late November.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: 1962 is the reference trade in Indian strategic memory: any Chinese diplomatic warmth is priced as potential cover for tactical positioning.

insights.claim: The Chinese account of 1962 is a 'self-defense counterattack' against Indian forward posts and suspected Indian efforts to peel Tibet away after the Dalai Lama's 1959 flight — and the months of Indian forward-post building that preceded the attack is not taught in Indian schools.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: Both national narratives are load-bearing and partial, so neither side's public framing of a border incident is a reliable read of what actually happened.
insights.locator: The Chinese have their own account of 1962

insights.claim: China's arming of Pakistan — demonstrated when Chinese-built J-10C fighters were deployed against Indian aircraft in aerial battles in May 2025 — is read in India not as normal alliance politics but as a deliberate encirclement strategy, hardening a settled conviction that China deploys dialogue as a screen for tactical advantage.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: Chinese defense exports to Pakistan are the single most reliable trigger for Indian escalation and procurement acceleration — a watch item for defense-industrial demand.
insights.quote: that China is a bad-faith actor, one that deploys dialogue as a screen for tactical advantage
insights.locator: More than 60 years on, the wound continues

insights.claim: India's self-image is not of a junior partner but of a civilizational creditor: Buddhism, which reshaped Chinese culture, philosophy, art and governance over two millennia, originated in India, and 'Journey to the West' is premised on a Chinese pilgrimage to India for Buddhist scriptures.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: Explains why economic-hierarchy arguments from Beijing reliably backfire in Delhi — status, not GDP, is the negotiating currency India defends.
insights.quote: If anything, from India’s perspective, China owes it a civilizational debt.

themes.theme: Information Blackout Between Delhi and Beijing

insights.claim: Tit-for-tat expulsions between 2016 and 2023 left, by 2024, a single Indian journalist for the Press Trust of India based in China and no Chinese journalists in India at all; one more Indian correspondent has since been added in Beijing and a single Xinhua correspondent is expected in New Delhi.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: Correspondent counts are a cheap, concrete leading indicator of whether the India-China thaw is real — watch visa restorations before believing summit language.

insights.claim: Two nuclear-armed neighbors that together hold a third of the world's population and share a 4,000-kilometer boundary still get the majority of their information about each other from third-party, usually Western, sources.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: Structural mispricing of each other's intentions raises the tail risk of miscalculation between two nuclear states — a fat-tail geopolitical risk that no market indicator captures.
insights.quote: is an indictment of the mutual failure of investment in understanding each other directly

insights.claim: When resident foreign correspondents disappear, the vacuum is filled by online trolls and 'professors from WhatsApp University' who generate reality-warping hyper-nationalism rather than reliable information about the other country.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: Public opinion in both countries is being formed by the least accurate sources, which constrains how far leaders can de-escalate without domestic cost.
insights.quote: In their place, we get online trolls and professors from WhatsApp University who often generate reality-warping hyper-nationalism and xenophobia rather than reliable information.

insights.claim: The India-China relationship has been sputtering into a reset since the 2020 Galwan Valley clashes, with the first delegation of senior Indian journalists to visit China in years and a Center for China and Globalization dialogue as the visible normalization markers.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: A thaw driven by think-tank meetings rather than institutional plumbing is reversible; size India-China trade and border-risk positions accordingly.
insights.locator: The dialogue, organized by the Center for China and Globalization

insights.claim: Both India and China are in the throes of an overheated nationalism that has been weaponized to distract from domestic troubles, capping how far any bilateral thaw can go.
insights.speaker: Pallavi Aiyar
insights.so_what: Domestic political incentives on both sides reward confrontation, so treat de-escalation headlines as tactical rather than structural.
insights.quote: Both countries are in the throes of an overheated nationalism that has been weaponized to distract from domestic troubles
insights.locator: Bringing back journalists will not erase
